objectives.name: Translate business problems into Claude-based AI solutions
Align solutions to business value pillars
Design system prompts, templates and guardrails
Apply zero-shot, few-shot and reasoning techniques
Optimize context windows and token usage
Implement caching, modular prompts and Skills
Match retrieval to data shape and queries
Select MCP, API/CLI or agent-to-agent mechanisms
Evaluate progressive discovery versus monolithic context
Define accuracy, latency, cost, safety and security metrics
Design datasets and mixed-method test frameworks
Conduct A/B tests and iterative improvements
Diagnose prompt failure, hallucinations and model mismatch
Monitor performance with logs and observability
Identify risks, limitations and failure modes
Support discovery, design, handoff, monitoring and iteration
Configure Claude tools and environments for teams

questions.title: A decision that the pilot can actually answer
questions.stem: An investigation prototype performs well on historical tickets, which exclude abandoned cases. A six-week pilot can observe live work but cannot change safety approvals. Which scope best tests whether integration saves enough engineer time?

options.text: Run on resolved historical tickets and extrapolate their time savings across all live investigations.
options.why: The resolved-only sample excludes the cases most likely to change the business estimate.

options.text: Compare representative live work, including abandonment and review, with a baseline; preserve safety approvals.
options.why: It measures the intended time outcome on the missing real-workload cases without altering safety authority.

options.text: Use volunteer experts' drafting speed and satisfaction to infer investigation savings across the whole organization.
options.why: Expert volunteers and generation speed do not establish representative investigation-time benefit.

options.text: Integrate broadly and defer investigation-time measurement until enough production incidents have completed successfully.
options.why: It commits to integration before collecting the evidence needed for that business decision.

questions.decision: The pilot must test the business hypothesis on the missing workload and full human effort, not only repeat a selectively successful technical demonstration.

questions.title: Outcome feedback without live learning
questions.stem: Dispatchers rate suggested delivery windows highly, but bookings happen elsewhere and detention-charge savings are unknown. Pseudonymous shipment linkage is allowed for 30 days. Which TWO additions best establish accountable business impact?

options.text: Link versioned suggestions and decisions to shipment outcomes, including charges and unsuccessful scheduling.
options.why: It connects advice to the downstream outcome, including failures that ratings alone miss.

options.text: Retain more raw conversations and compare suggestion counts with depot visits.
options.why: More raw data and counts do not create the required suggestion-to-outcome linkage.

options.text: Assign an operations owner to review outcome slices, select regressions and approve controlled changes.
options.why: An owner converts outcome evidence into accountable changes rather than uncontrolled feedback ingestion.

options.text: Replace dispatcher ratings with a judge of how persuasive suggestions sound.
options.why: Persuasiveness does not establish reduced charges or improved actual scheduling outcomes.

options.text: Train nightly on accepted suggestions as sufficient correctness labels.
options.why: Acceptance is not proven downstream success; unreviewed updates also weaken release accountability.

questions.decision: The architectural gap is a measured output-to-outcome loop plus an owner who can safely act on it, within the stated retention boundary.

questions.title: When a bounded agent is justified
questions.stem: Material-failure research follows unpredictable evidence branches. A fixed workflow is brittle. Only read-only exploration is allowed; findings need citations and work has a strict budget. Which architecture best supports accountable termination?

options.text: Use a read-only agent with separate branch budgets but unlimited new branches.
options.why: Per-branch limits do not enforce the strict total work budget when the number of branches is unpredictable.

options.text: Use approved reads, evidence contracts, a total budget and clear stopping and escalation rules.
options.why: Adaptive branching is genuinely needed; bounded tools and stopping rules preserve the stated scope and resource limits.

options.text: Use one fixed evidence packet and escalate every unexpected read need.
options.why: A fixed packet turns the recurring unpredictable evidence needs into avoidable manual interruptions instead of supporting bounded exploration.

options.text: Retain explicit branches and add each new evidence pattern before automated continuation.
options.why: It keeps the demonstrated brittle enumeration requirement even though evidence-dependent branch structure is unpredictable.

questions.decision: Variable input alone does not justify autonomy, but demonstrated unpredictable evidence-dependent exploration can; retain bounded authority, evidence, and termination contracts.

questions.title: Parallel analysis with controlled synthesis
questions.stem: Competition, contract and migration specialists have separate approved corpora. Entity-ID mismatches cause conflicting conclusions. The final report must expose conflicts and stay within budget. Which THREE orchestration choices best fit?

options.text: Load all corpora into identical generalists and vote on the report.
options.why: Shared unrestricted corpora violate access constraints and voting does not resolve mismatched identifiers.

options.text: Reconcile IDs centrally and display incompatible findings with provenance.
options.why: Conflicting entity interpretations require explicit resolution or escalation, not ungrounded consensus.

options.text: Bound retries and total work; return partial coverage when budget runs out.
options.why: A bounded partial report preserves budget and makes coverage gaps visible.

options.text: Let specialists exchange unrestricted excerpts and limit coordination to formatting.
options.why: Direct exchange violates the stated corpus access boundary despite potentially faster reconciliation.

options.text: Give specialists scoped tasks, entity IDs, evidence/uncertainty fields and only approved corpus access.
options.why: Contracts let independent results be compared without granting unnecessary cross-corpus access.

questions.decision: Parallelize independent expertise, standardize the evidence interface, and retain explicit reconciliation and resource boundaries at the coordinator.

questions.title: Decomposition that preserves dependencies
questions.stem: A rail planner interprets inspection narratives well but assigns crews to overlapping locations. Crew and track-access constraints are structured and exact. Which decomposition best preserves language interpretation while improving schedule reliability?

options.text: Have crew/access agents make local plans and a writer merge them.
options.why: Independently valid plans can conflict jointly; a writing merge does not enforce coupled constraints.

options.text: Generate three complete plans and choose the most coherent by model judge.
options.why: Coherence voting cannot establish exact nonoverlap when structured validation is available.

options.text: Split narratives equally and concatenate recommended work in report order.
options.why: Token boundaries ignore shared crews and track windows, retaining the underlying global conflict.

options.text: Extract cited needs, schedule deterministically, then explain feasible work and unresolved exceptions.
options.why: It separates interpretation from exact joint constraint solving and explains only validated feasible plans.

questions.decision: Decomposition must preserve the dependencies that make a solution valid; exact cross-task constraints belong in an explicit validation or solving step.

questions.title: Capacity savings after review cost
questions.stem: For 6,000 monthly cases, preparation falls from 12 to four staff minutes but adds two verification minutes. Other work, volume and rework are unchanged. What monthly capacity gain is supported before staffing decisions?

options.text: 800 hours; exclude verification as an existing oversight responsibility.
options.why: Verification is explicitly added by the pilot; excluding it overstates capacity gain by 200 hours.

options.text: 1,200 hours; count the entire original workload as automated.
options.why: Four preparation and two verification minutes remain for every case, so the full baseline is not released.

options.text: 600 hours; assess cash savings separately against staffing, demand and costs.
options.why: Net saving is six minutes per case, totaling 36,000 minutes or 600 hours; cash savings are not automatic.

options.text: 600 hours; payroll should fall equivalently once the pilot reaches volume.
options.why: The capacity arithmetic is right, but payroll reduction requires a staffing or expenditure change not supplied.

questions.decision: Count all changed human work before estimating benefit. Six thousand times six minutes divided by sixty is 600 hours; capacity is distinct from cash.

questions.title: When a useful non-agent answer wins
questions.stem: Four approved leaflets total 9,000 tokens, share access rights and change twice yearly. Supplied-document answers pass quality/latency gates; no live data or actions are needed. Which TWO choices best fit?

options.text: Add update and customer-record tools now to anticipate transactional expansion.
options.why: Unused transactional authority expands scope and attack surface beyond the approved question-answering task.

options.text: Version documents, prompts and acceptance cases; revisit retrieval if size, access or freshness changes.
options.why: Versioning supports safe maintenance and defines concrete triggers for revisiting the simpler architecture.

options.text: Use web research whenever the assistant is unsure about leaflet answers.
options.why: Unapproved outside material changes the evidence boundary despite no current information gap requiring web research.

options.text: Require embeddings and snippet retrieval even when the approved corpus fits efficiently.
options.why: Retrieval adds a new failure surface without a demonstrated need or benefit under the stated pilot evidence.

options.text: Start with an augmented call, versioned leaflets, citations and abstention for unsupported details.
options.why: The measured context-based approach satisfies current needs without an unnecessary retrieval or action layer.

questions.decision: Choose the simplest architecture demonstrated to meet requirements, but preserve versioned evidence and specific conditions under which the decision should change.

questions.title: A correlated consensus failure
questions.stem: Three subsidy reviewers share a retrieved excerpt whose exception clause was truncated. All agree on the wrong decision. What is the smallest correction addressing this failure without multiplying routine cost?

options.text: Vary reviewer wording and temperature while retaining majority approval.
options.why: Different wording does not restore the missing exception or establish independent evidence.

options.text: Add two reviewers using the same excerpt and require four votes.
options.why: More votes on the same incomplete evidence preserve the correlated failure and increase routine cost.

options.text: Keep reviews and emphasize minority concerns in the coordinator's wording.
options.why: There was no informed minority; formatting cannot create evidence that every reviewer lacked.

options.text: Validate eligibility evidence before review; route missing/conflicting clauses to exceptions.
options.why: The shared missing evidence is the causal failure; gating completeness addresses it before correlated decisions occur.

questions.decision: Multiple model calls are not independent safeguards when they share the same defective evidence. Repair the common dependency.

questions.title: A recoverable external effect
questions.stem: An invitation assistant drafts, obtains organizer approval and sends mail. Timeouts sometimes occur after acceptance, causing duplicate retries. Organizers retain authority over wording and recipients. Which TWO changes best support recovery?

options.text: Bind approval to draft and recipient; renew it for material changes but allow safe identical retries.
options.why: It preserves organizer authority without treating an unchanged transport retry as a new content decision.

options.text: Disable retries and label every timeout unsuccessful for manual resending.
options.why: It can trigger duplicate manual sends and falsely labels an uncertain external outcome as definite failure.

options.text: Generate a new draft and ID for each retry under the original general approval.
options.why: Fresh identifiers defeat deduplication, and changed wording is not the approved content.

options.text: Persist the approved invitation and operation ID; use idempotent sending or reconcile status before retrying.
options.why: A durable operation identity prevents blind duplicate effects when timeout leaves the outcome uncertain.

options.text: Infer delivery from the assistant's prior explanation after a timeout.
options.why: Language-model inference is not evidence of the external service’s committed delivery state.

questions.decision: Separate approved intent, durable execution identity, and uncertain external outcome. Recovery should reconcile state rather than recreate intent.

questions.title: Accuracy gates before a cheaper cascade
questions.stem: Every released language needs ≥95% routing accuracy and completion p95 below three seconds. The exhibit includes routing overhead on one held-out workload. Minimize cost after both gates. Which design should launch?

options.text: Large: superior correctness justifies higher cost even though other candidates pass.
options.why: Extra correctness has no stated priority after the gates; balanced meets them more cheaply.

options.text: Balanced: all language/latency gates pass at the lowest feasible cost.
options.why: The cascade fails the minority-language gate; the larger single model is feasible but costs more than balanced.

options.text: Cascade: adjust escalation and assume minority accuracy reaches Balanced's result.
options.why: A threshold hypothesis needs measurement; assumed slice improvement does not establish release readiness.

options.text: Cascade: pooled accuracy passes and measured cost is lowest.
options.why: The requirement applies to each language, so the pooled result cannot conceal the failing language slice.

questions.decision: Apply the actual slice-level quality gate before optimizing cost. A well-designed cascade remains a candidate until its measured weaknesses are repaired.

questions.title: Partitioning an evidence-heavy investigation
questions.stem: Thousands of supplier disclosures exceed combined context. Summary chains lose minority findings. Every material discrepancy needs citations, and omitted findings cannot imply no discrepancy. Asynchronous work is allowed. Which design best fits?

options.text: Repeatedly summarize fixed-length document paragraphs until the corpus fits.
options.why: Repeated compression can erase minority discrepancies and lacks explicit coverage or evidence-preservation guarantees.

options.text: Read longest disclosures first and label unsampled suppliers discrepancy-free.
options.why: Unsampled material has not been reviewed; the proposal violates the requirement about unsupported absence.

options.text: Read sequentially while carrying forward only a recommendation and confidence.
options.why: A current narrative and confidence estimate do not preserve traceable findings or coverage across thousands of documents.

options.text: Track obligation/supplier coverage and cited findings, then reconcile cross-partition discrepancies.
options.why: Obligation-based partitioning and coverage records retain evidence and expose unreviewed areas instead of equating omission with absence.

questions.decision: Decompose around the comparison unit and preserve both positive findings and coverage evidence; summaries alone are not a completeness mechanism.

questions.title: The model route must be measurable
questions.stem: A cascade labels 30% of requests difficult. Only that route was evaluated; finance assumes the cheap route is equally accurate. Production requires ≥96% end-to-end correctness. What evidence is needed next?

options.text: Deploy because routing sends easier cases to the cheap model by design.
options.why: A label of easier is not evidence that the cheaper path meets the required quality.

options.text: Evaluate the full held-out production mix, including routing errors, overhead and critical slices.
options.why: End-to-end evaluation includes the untested easy path and routing mistakes that could invalidate the business gate.

options.text: Compare models on difficult cases only and choose routine routing by input price.
options.why: Difficult-only testing cannot establish accuracy for the majority path; unit pricing omits routing overhead.

options.text: Escalate 50% and assume broader large-model coverage guarantees correctness.
options.why: More escalation may help, but an arbitrary fraction does not prove the required system result.

questions.decision: A model-routing architecture includes the router and every downstream path; measure the complete system rather than its best-tested component.

questions.title: Examples disagree with the policy
questions.stem: An export classifier's policy requires escalation for ambiguous destinations, but old examples approve them. Outputs are inconsistent despite valid schemas. Which TWO actions best repair behavior and verify routine cases still work?

options.text: Test held-out ambiguous and routine cases for escalation behavior and schema validity.
options.why: The test checks the actual policy behavior and prevents a fix from degrading routine cases.

options.text: Release when explanations fluently identify which example was trusted.
options.why: An articulate explanation can justify the wrong policy and is not evidence of correct escalation behavior.

options.text: Correct contradictory examples and separate task instructions from request content.
options.why: Contradictory examples create competing behavioral guidance; alignment and separation address that prompt-level cause.

options.text: Move contradictory examples earlier to give more reconciliation space.
options.why: Reordering does not eliminate the policy contradiction or establish the intended authoritative behavior.

options.text: Remove escalation from the schema, permitting only approval or rejection.
options.why: It removes the expressly required ambiguous-case escalation and sacrifices semantic correctness for schema consistency.

questions.decision: Resolve inconsistent guidance and test the targeted behavior. Valid structure and fluent explanations do not establish compliance with the approved policy.

questions.title: Compact the history without rewriting authority
questions.stem: Repeated compaction loses an unresolved legal restriction in an account-research session. Current constraints and evidence matter; old results are retrievable, and changing the restriction requires authorization. Which context strategy best supports correct continuation?

options.text: Increase output allowance to restate more history every reply.
options.why: More output consumes budget and does not establish faithful retention of the critical restriction.

options.text: Drop earlier messages and assume users will repeat important restrictions.
options.why: The unresolved restriction remains binding even when the latest request does not repeat it.

options.text: Use one persuasive summary as the sole remaining authority.
options.why: A narrative can silently omit restrictions and makes accumulated compression the authority instead of approved source decisions.

options.text: Keep validated constraints, open decisions and evidence links; retrieve compacted historical details.
options.why: It distinguishes durable authority and open decisions from disposable history, while preserving evidence access and checking compaction fidelity.

questions.decision: Compaction should preserve explicit current constraints and provenance, with checks for lost authority; chronology and narrative smoothness are secondary.

questions.title: Correct ordering but inconsistent tool schemas
questions.stem: An eligible stable prefix precedes case text; requests arrive each minute within a five-minute cache lifetime. Writes remain frequent because generated tool descriptions vary each request, though behavior is unchanged. Which TWO actions target this cause?

options.text: Replace schemas with names and infer argument contracts from prior calls.
options.why: It removes the registered execution contract and compromises supported tool behavior to improve cache metrics.

options.text: Canonicalize/version unchanged definitions so schemas and descriptions have identical bytes.
options.why: Tool definitions precede policy in the cached prefix; unnecessary textual variation breaks exact prefix reuse.

options.text: Replay fixed definitions and compare cache reads/writes and selection quality, retaining intentional version changes.
options.why: A controlled replay tests the identified variable and ensures optimization does not freeze legitimate capability changes.

options.text: Extend lifetime while keeping minute-by-minute tool-definition variation.
options.why: Requests already arrive within the stated lifetime; different prefix bytes remain a separate invalidation cause.

options.text: Move case text farther back while retaining regenerated tool descriptions.
options.why: The varying tool definitions still occur before the reusable policy, so later dynamic placement does not fix the mismatch.

questions.decision: Cache eligibility and ordering are necessary but insufficient: exact stable bytes include tool definitions before policy. Isolate changed prefix material with telemetry.

questions.title: Reasoning detail has a cost
questions.stem: A contract assistant must return a risk label, cited justification and reviewer question. Exhaustive visible reasoning raises cost and latency without improving quality. Legal needs evidence, not internal reasoning transcripts. What change best fits?

options.text: Return only the label, dropping justification and reviewer questions.
options.why: It cuts required output and legal evidence rather than the unnecessary exhaustive reasoning requirement.

options.text: Generate two exhaustive drafts and summarize them with a smaller model.
options.why: Extra drafts multiply work without measured quality benefit and retain the unnecessary analysis cost.

options.text: Stream exhaustive reasoning earlier and treat first-token speed as completion compliance.
options.why: Streaming can improve perceived responsiveness without reducing total generation time or proving completion targets.

options.text: Return required structured fields with concise cited justification; retest quality and latency.
options.why: The output contract meets legal needs while removing unhelpful verbosity demonstrated to add cost and latency.

questions.decision: Optimize the required output contract against evidence; useful justification is distinct from demanding a long customer-visible reasoning trace.

questions.title: A long document is not always a long-context task
questions.stem: Manual questions name a clause and referenced table 92% of the time. Retrieval reliably finds both; comparisons need broader context. Entire manuals are currently sent. Which TWO changes best reduce input cost without losing coverage?

options.text: Use the longest-context model for all requests and cap output.
options.why: Shorter output does not remove unnecessary input cost and may restrict required answers.

options.text: Retain an evaluated broad-context fallback; monitor insufficiency and routing errors by query class.
options.why: The minority pattern has different evidence needs and must not silently inherit the narrow-context assumption.

options.text: Summarize manuals without section IDs and use short matches for all comparisons.
options.why: Removing identifiers and reference relationships threatens coverage for precise clauses and cross-section comparison.

options.text: Truncate to opening pages and fill missing clauses from model knowledge.
options.why: Clause-specific evidence may occur anywhere, and general knowledge cannot replace the required citations.

options.text: Use validated clause/reference retrieval with tables and provenance for specific questions.
options.why: The common query names a known evidence unit; targeted retrieval reduces context while preserving supporting references.

questions.decision: Match context construction to query shape, preserve references, and explicitly evaluate the routing boundary rather than applying a universal truncation rule.

questions.title: Skills without hidden universal context
questions.stem: Eleven specialist procedures overwhelm context, though most tasks need one. Short descriptions identify applicability, but a universal safety baseline always applies. Which progressive-disclosure design best fits?

options.text: Replace procedures with one generic example and infer specialist workflows.
options.why: A generic example discards the approved task-specific guidance rather than disclosing it progressively.

options.text: Keep the baseline durable, expose brief descriptions and load needed specialist details.
options.why: It preserves universal constraints while making optional specialized detail available on demand.

options.text: Load all procedures every turn and instruct the model to ignore irrelevant ones.
options.why: Ignoring irrelevant text does not recover the consumed context or reduce interference.

options.text: Defer everything, including the baseline, behind specialist selection.
options.why: The baseline becomes conditional on successful discovery and loading, contrary to its universal requirement.

questions.decision: Progressive disclosure is appropriate for optional detail, while genuinely universal authority must remain reliably available independent of specialty selection.

questions.title: A near-miss extraction example
questions.stem: An invoice extractor returns issue dates when shipment dates are absent. Its date-or-null schema is correct, but examples show matching issue/shipment dates. Which smallest prompt change targets the error while preserving real extraction?

options.text: Rename the field while retaining matching-date examples and no missing-field guidance.
options.why: A better name alone leaves the demonstrated ambiguity in every example and no explicit absence behavior.

options.text: Ask for longer date explanations and accept those mentioning shipping.
options.why: An explanation can rationalize the same wrong field and does not resolve the missing-evidence contract.

options.text: Add distinct-date and absent-shipment examples; require null without shipment evidence.
options.why: Contrasts teach the specific distinction and missing-evidence behavior without changing the valid schema.

options.text: Require a date and explicitly substitute issue date when shipment date is missing.
options.why: The substitution changes the business semantics and removes the existing valid null response.

questions.decision: Use discriminating examples that exercise the near-miss and absent-evidence cases; extra wording is useful only when it clarifies the actual distinction.

questions.title: Capability pruning before better selection
questions.stem: A read-only inventory assistant retains eight purchasing-write tools and credentials from a prototype alongside 12 reads. Similar names cause selection errors. Which change first enforces the role and simplifies capabilities?

options.text: Add warning prefixes and examples favoring inventory reads.
options.why: Naming may reduce confusion but retains unauthorized capabilities and their credentials.

options.text: Label writes emergency-only and require an explanation before use.
options.why: Descriptions and explanations leave forbidden write capabilities reachable and do not enforce the read-only role.

options.text: Remove purchasing tools/write credentials, then tune read-tool descriptions on representative requests.
options.why: It removes unnecessary action authority and selection candidates, then addresses remaining usability issues.

options.text: Hide writes behind a selector but retain credentials for unusual discrepancies.
options.why: An inferred unusual request is not authority to expand an explicitly read-only role.

questions.decision: Prune capabilities that the role cannot use before optimizing discovery or descriptions of the capabilities that remain.

questions.title: Authentication stops at the wrong boundary
questions.stem: An MCP server validates identity and audience, then fetches any supplied account ID with a service credential. Only assigned managers may view each account. Which TWO controls close the remaining authorization gap?

options.text: Scope service access, bind account selection to validated authorization and log denials without content.
options.why: Defense in depth limits service reach and makes unauthorized attempts observable without leaking data.

options.text: Have Claude compare account IDs with self-reported job titles.
options.why: A user-stated title and model judgment are not server-enforced account authorization.

options.text: Extend token expiry to reduce manager authentication interruptions.
options.why: Longer validity improves convenience but does not evaluate the missing account assignment.

options.text: Accept all company tokens because signature and audience already passed.
options.why: Company membership and token validity do not confer permission to every protected account.

options.text: Check the authenticated principal's current account assignment before each protected read.
options.why: A valid identity must still be authorized for the specific resource and operation.

questions.decision: Authentication establishes who called; authorization determines whether that caller may perform this operation on this account at execution time.

questions.title: Accuracy at a fixed completion deadline
questions.stem: Release requires supported answers ≥96% and completed-response p95 ≤2.4 seconds. The exhibit includes reranking and generation on a representative workload with identical access controls. Minimize cost after gates pass. Which configuration should launch?

options.text: Ridge: greater support offsets a modest latency overrun.
options.why: The contract contains a latency gate; a quality gain does not authorize exceeding it.

options.text: Valley: lowest cost and fastest completion outweigh a small support deficit.
options.why: Close to the threshold is insufficient when the agreed gate requires at least 96% support.

options.text: Harbor: both service gates pass at the lowest eligible cost.
options.why: Harbor costs less than Summit; Valley fails support and Ridge fails latency.

options.text: Summit: strongest support within latency, regardless of the cost objective.
options.why: Both Harbor and Summit pass, so the explicit cost objective favors Harbor.

questions.decision: Treat contractual quality and tail latency as independent gates, then minimize cost using measured end-to-end results rather than isolated stages.

questions.title: A distributed trace with restricted content
questions.stem: A retail assistant spans gateway, retrieval, Claude and an order API across three teams. Customers report slow answers despite acceptable component averages. Payment details cannot enter telemetry. Which THREE observability changes best support diagnosis?

options.text: Share complete prompts, customer records and payment payloads for reconstruction.
options.why: Immediate convenience does not override the explicit prohibition on raw payment data in telemetry.

options.text: Keep component averages and page everyone when any chosen threshold is exceeded.
options.why: Uncorrelated averages cannot identify the critical path, and arbitrary alerts do not resolve the measurement gap.

options.text: Redact at collection, retain allowed metadata and assign alert/incident-response ownership.
options.why: It preserves useful diagnostics without violating the content boundary and makes response accountable.

options.text: Propagate request IDs across spans with timing, outcomes and parent/dependency relationships.
options.why: Correlated spans reveal which dependencies and paths compose the actual slow operation.

options.text: Measure end-to-end and stage tails by workload slice, retaining configuration versions.
options.why: Tails and versioned slices expose regressions that averages can conceal.

questions.decision: Customer latency is a correlated system property; operational evidence should retain timings and version context while excluding prohibited content.

questions.title: The correct clause at the wrong time
questions.stem: Lease chunks preserve structure and dates, but retrieval uses renewal terms for earlier accounting periods. Historical versions must remain searchable. Which change targets the defect without deleting valid history?

options.text: Delete superseded clauses and use current terms for all periods.
options.why: Deleting valid historical evidence violates the requirement to answer earlier-period questions.

options.text: Filter lease/effective intervals, preserve supersession links and cite period-applicable clauses.
options.why: The missing constraint is temporal applicability, not chunk structure; both historical and current versions remain useful.

options.text: Increase overlap while keeping version-agnostic selection unchanged.
options.why: More local context does not choose the effective version for the requested period.

options.text: Merge all terms into one summary and always cite the latest amendment.
options.why: A merged latest-version summary can silently apply current terms to a historical question.

questions.decision: Good chunk boundaries do not settle which version applies. Match temporal and entity constraints explicitly while preserving valid historical evidence.

questions.title: Aggregation over a structured relationship
questions.stem: A quarterly spend query needs Company L's subsidiaries, ownership dates, Supplier R identities, currencies and deduplicated invoices. Dense retrieval misses subsidiaries and duplicates amounts. Policy text lives separately. Which TWO changes best support authorized totals?

options.text: Return calculated totals with period, relationship assumptions and record lineage; explain alongside policy evidence.
options.why: It preserves computation evidence and keeps explanatory policy retrieval distinct from the authoritative numeric result.

options.text: Fill context with more invoice matches and let Claude infer complete coverage.
options.why: A larger similarity sample does not establish relational completeness or reliable duplicate elimination.

options.text: Use an authorized calculation/query service for ownership intervals, deduplication, currency normalization and quarterly aggregation.
options.why: The query requires complete relational filtering and exact aggregation rather than a handful of similar text excerpts.

options.text: Sum the first keyword matches for Supplier R as the authoritative total.
options.why: Keyword matching does not enforce ownership intervals, currency normalization, or unique invoice identity.

options.text: Add annual-report summaries assuming common ownership periods and quarters.
options.why: The assumptions ignore ownership dates and accounting periods, so the aggregation can count inapplicable evidence.

questions.decision: Match retrieval to the data operation: entity relationships, time intervals, deduplication, and sums belong in a governed structured computation, with language used for explanation.

questions.title: A stable backend does not need discovery
questions.stem: Nightly billing reconciliation calls two stable typed APIs using a dedicated service identity. It has no interactive assistant or runtime discovery need. Which integration best fits before adopting another team's desktop MCP approach?

options.text: Add MCP and reuse broad desktop-user tokens for inherited access.
options.why: Interactive user authority is not an appropriate default service identity and adds unnecessary capability reach.

options.text: Use administrator-backed shell access to avoid restrictive API contracts.
options.why: Bypassing typed contracts and scoped identity sacrifices controls without satisfying any stated need.

options.text: Have agents negotiate reconciliation through an agent-to-agent conversation.
options.why: A stable deterministic integration has no demonstrated need for negotiated autonomous coordination.

options.text: Use scoped typed APIs, retries and monitoring; add MCP for demonstrated interoperability needs.
options.why: The workload has stable direct contracts and no current discovery or assistant-client requirement.

questions.decision: Choose protocols for the actual client and contract requirements; a useful assistant protocol is not automatically the best backend service interface.

questions.title: Discovery should preserve essential routing tools
questions.stem: Deferring 460 tools cuts context but sometimes hides a small task-status tool required on every resume path. Most tasks need only a few tools. Which TWO changes preserve deferral's benefit while addressing this failure?

options.text: Test discovery recall, loading cost, selection and completion latency on new and resumed jobs.
options.why: The evaluation covers both the original efficiency goal and the newly exposed resume failure.

options.text: Expose essential status directly; defer specialized tools behind clear discovery entries.
options.why: Universal resume functionality need not depend on discovery; specialized schemas retain their context savings.

options.text: Keep everything deferred and list every possible resume phrase in the system prompt.
options.why: Exhaustive phrasing increases context and still makes essential status access depend on successful discovery.

options.text: Load every specialized schema on all resume requests.
options.why: It restores the large context burden instead of isolating the small universally needed interface.

options.text: Remove status access and infer completion from saved job descriptions.
options.why: A saved narrative is not an authoritative current status source for an external long-running operation.

questions.decision: Deferral is selective: keep small essential interfaces immediate, discover optional detail, and evaluate the resume path rather than only new-task success.

questions.title: A token forwarded to the wrong resource
questions.stem: An MCP server forwards its own incoming token to a document API requiring a different audience. Both trust one identity provider, but acceptance varies by environment. Which repair respects resource-specific authorization?

options.text: Remove MCP audience checks because a trusted signature establishes authority.
options.why: Issuer trust alone does not show that the token is intended for the receiving resource.

options.text: Make the document API accept both audiences to normalize forwarding.
options.why: Broadening accepted audiences to accommodate passthrough weakens resource separation rather than establishing proper delegation.

options.text: Validate MCP audience, authorize downstream separately and enforce document permissions.
options.why: Resource audience and downstream delegation are distinct; each boundary requires appropriate authorization.

options.text: Keep forwarding and use one user access confirmation per session.
options.why: User confirmation does not change token audience or prove document authorization at the downstream API.

questions.decision: A token is not a universal identity pass. Validate resource intent and establish appropriate downstream authority instead of passing through incompatible credentials.

questions.title: Parallel reads without speculative writes
questions.stem: Supplier and shipment reads are independent, authorized and idempotent. Ordering requires both results and an approved draft; speculative writes are forbidden. Reads dominate latency. Which TWO changes best shorten the critical path?

options.text: Approve a generic template before evidence arrives and draft in parallel.
options.why: Generic approval does not bind the eventual evidence-dependent transaction that will execute.

options.text: Remove one read because similar latency suggests redundant information.
options.why: Equal latency says nothing about whether the two sources provide interchangeable evidence.

options.text: Keep placement behind validation/approval with stable operation identity and uncertain-outcome recovery.
options.why: The consequential effect remains dependent on the required results and approved intent.

options.text: Run reads concurrently, joining both results before drafting and validation.
options.why: Parallel independent reads remove unnecessary sequential delay without bypassing result dependencies.

options.text: Place orders alongside reads and cancel them if evidence later raises concerns.
options.why: Cancellation may occur after an irreversible external effect and violates the no-speculation requirement.

questions.decision: Parallelize tasks whose inputs and effects permit it; do not turn dependent or consequential work into speculative execution merely to shorten latency.

questions.title: Revocation in a derived index
questions.stem: Project access is revoked immediately at source, but a nightly vector refresh leaves old chunks retrievable. Revocation must apply before the next query, independent of content updates. Which design meets this requirement?

options.text: Refresh the index hourly and document that access-list changes usually propagate within the improved interval.
options.why: Any positive interval can still violate the requirement that revocation precede the next query.

options.text: Encrypt the index at rest while retaining current retrieval permissions because stored data is protected.
options.why: At-rest encryption does not stop an unauthorized query from receiving decrypted project chunks.

options.text: Ask Claude to omit project information when users mention changed roles, retaining existing index behavior.
options.why: User disclosure and prompt obedience are not an enforced check against the current access list.

options.text: Check current access before exposing candidates; maintain content changes and deletions separately.
options.why: Current authorization blocks stale-index disclosure without assuming immediate content refresh.

questions.decision: Content freshness and authorization freshness are different contracts. A stale content index must not become the authority for current resource access.

questions.title: The monitoring cardinality trap
questions.stem: Metrics label every event with full user text and document/request IDs. Costs spike, dashboards stall and sensitive labels violate privacy expectations. Responders need aggregate trends and permitted request diagnosis. Which design best supports both?

options.text: Hash text labels and retain all IDs to solve cost and privacy.
options.why: Distinct hashes retain high cardinality, and hashing is not an automatic privacy or retention justification.

options.text: Use bounded aggregate metrics and restricted correlated traces; exclude sensitive text.
options.why: It controls metric cardinality while retaining authorized request investigation and minimizing sensitive data.

options.text: Keep labels but display dashboards daily to reduce stored data.
options.why: Dashboard sampling does not remove the underlying high-cardinality series or prohibited text collection.

options.text: Remove all identifiers from metrics and traces, keeping global averages only.
options.why: It discards the required ability to investigate an individual permitted request and hides tail behavior.

questions.decision: Use bounded metric labels for trends and controlled traces for request detail; collection minimization must precede storage rather than rely on dashboard presentation.

questions.title: The success metric rewards abandonment
questions.stem: An assistant improves closure-without-transfer rates, but disputed bills rise as customers abandon unsupported explanations. Accurate resolution and safe escalation matter. Which evaluation best detects this failure?

options.text: Measure groundedness, latency and model cost without linking outcomes to later disputes.
options.why: Grounded communication can still fail to resolve the issue; the downstream resolution and dispute outcome remains unmeasured.

options.text: Gate verified resolution/disputes, groundedness, safe escalation, latency and total handling cost.
options.why: It evaluates actual service success and recognizes appropriate escalation rather than treating every closure as success.

options.text: Count closure without transfer as resolution and audit only transferred cases.
options.why: Closed and abandoned cases remain unaudited, preserving the exact false-success channel and incomplete cost boundary.

options.text: Survey completers and exclude abandonment because no final rating exists.
options.why: Excluding abandonment removes the cases that reveal the demonstrated harm and biases the outcome estimate.

questions.decision: A proxy that rewards premature closure needs outcome-based correction. Appropriate escalation can be a successful safety behavior rather than an evaluation failure.

questions.title: An evaluation set with repeated evidence
questions.stem: Random splits place paraphrases from the same policy paragraphs in development and test. Scores are high, but unseen policy families fail. Which TWO dataset changes best test generalization while preserving useful regressions?

options.text: Move failing new-family cases into development and report only stable tests.
options.why: Removing hard cases from evaluation hides the exact deployment risk that needs measurement.

options.text: Generate more paraphrases under the same split to dilute overlap.
options.why: More correlated paraphrases increase volume without correcting the leakage boundary.

options.text: Keep known-case regressions separate from new-family challenges with reviewed critical cases and provenance.
options.why: Distinct slices retain regression protection while measuring new-family and risk-sensitive capability.

options.text: Split by source family/policy group to prevent evidence and paraphrase leakage.
options.why: Grouping prevents the leakage that makes random question-level splitting overstate generalization.

options.text: Use model-generated expected labels instead of expert policy review.
options.why: Self-labeling cannot establish correctness and can preserve the model’s systematic exception errors.

questions.decision: Generalization is about unseen evidence groups, not just unseen wording. Keep regression and challenge evidence separate and preserve independently grounded labels.

questions.title: Conversation turns contaminate the experiment
questions.stem: Message-level A/B assignment mixes prompts within conversations. The new prompt benefits from clarification already done by the old one. Decisions concern full customer-case outcomes. Which redesign addresses this contamination?

options.text: Assign each whole conversation to one version; use prespecified gates and conversation-level outcomes.
options.why: Stable conversation assignment aligns treatment with the outcome and prevents versions from sharing one conversation’s causal history.

options.text: Keep message randomization and increase sample size to remove the late-message advantage.
options.why: Larger samples do not remove systematic treatment contamination or misaligned outcome units.

options.text: Ask a judge to infer causation from blended transcripts and treat confidence as significance.
options.why: A judge’s causal guess cannot repair the contaminated assignment design.

options.text: Use the new prompt only for final messages and compare them with earlier old-prompt ratings.
options.why: Different conversation stages remain confounded and do not identify the effect on complete case outcomes.

questions.decision: Choose the experimental unit that matches the decision and preserves a consistent treatment history; more observations do not fix an invalid assignment unit.

questions.title: Three kinds of evidence for an agent
questions.stem: A travel assistant claims reservation changes that sometimes never reach the database. Other valid changes have confusing confirmations. A generic final-message judge is the only current check. Which TWO additions separate execution success from communication quality?

options.text: Calibrate a task-specific communication rubric with human review, separate from state checks.
options.why: Human-calibrated judgment evaluates subjective communication without replacing objective outcome verification.

options.text: Add general judges and replace database checks when they agree.
options.why: Consensus about the narrative is still not evidence of actual booking state.

options.text: Count any booking-tool invocation as successful completion.
options.why: Invocation may fail or change the wrong state; activity count is not outcome verification.

options.text: Check isolated booking state and allowed effects deterministically for requested and unauthorized changes.
options.why: External state proves task outcome more directly than a convincing final message.

options.text: Treat repeated matching reservation IDs as proof of execution.
options.why: The same identifier can appear even when no external state change occurred.

questions.decision: Verify observable outcomes with deterministic state evidence and evaluate subjective communication with calibrated rubrics; neither should stand in for the other.

questions.title: A retrieval failure that looks like reasoning
questions.stem: The exhibit compares identical filing questions across index replays. Model and prompt are unchanged; only updated filings degrade with the new index. What should diagnosis inspect FIRST?

options.text: Roll back the unchanged model first, prioritizing the most visible AI component during incident response.
options.why: The unchanged model is not the demonstrated changed dependency, and replay evidence points to the index.

options.text: Inspect updated-filings ingestion/retrieval, using verified excerpts to control for generation.
options.why: Restored performance with verified excerpts isolates the changed evidence pipeline as the first likely failure layer.

options.text: Increase reasoning budget for all requests because updated filings require deeper analysis than older ones.
options.why: The verified-excerpt control shows the unchanged model can answer those cases well with correct evidence.

options.text: Demand stronger prompt confidence, treating new-index errors as excessive caution about recent financial evidence.
options.why: Confidence wording does not explain the observed index-dependent correctness collapse.

questions.decision: Use controlled replay to localize the failure. A generator that recovers with verified evidence does not justify model replacement as the first intervention.

questions.title: A feedback event is not a training label
questions.stem: Thumbs-down feedback mixes factual errors, dislike of correct policy and spam. A developer wants nightly prompt training on every negative case. Which TWO steps best support responsive, controlled iteration?

options.text: Regression-test affected/unaffected slices, apply release gates and deploy versioned changes with rollback ownership.
options.why: Controlled release prevents local fixes from silently degrading other behavior and preserves accountability.

options.text: Triage with source/version context; confirm labels and policy intent before selecting evaluation cases.
options.why: The event is ambiguous; classification and verification distinguish correctness problems from dissatisfaction or abuse.

options.text: Minimize negatives by softening mandatory restrictions users dislike.
options.why: Fewer complaints can result from violating policy, so the metric cannot substitute for correctness and safety gates.

options.text: Turn every negative rating into an opposite-answer example.
options.why: Negative feedback does not establish that the answer or policy was incorrect.

options.text: Hide disputed cases until policy review while engineers adjust style.
options.why: It conceals potentially material errors rather than collecting and resolving the evidence.

questions.decision: Feedback initiates investigation; it is not self-validating supervision. Curate evidence, test changes across slices, and close the loop through controlled releases.

questions.title: Choose a cache lifetime for bursty reuse
questions.stem: Use the fictional charges and three ten-request bursts in the exhibit. No eviction or prefix changes occur; dynamic/output costs are identical. Which lifetime minimizes total prefix cost?

options.text: One hour: three writes and 27 reads cost $0.174 because every burst rewrites.
options.why: The prefix is still cached at minutes twenty and forty under the one-hour lifetime, so those are reads.

options.text: Five minutes: one write and 29 reads cost $0.083 because prefix text is shared.
options.why: Identical text does not prevent expiration across gaps longer than five minutes.

options.text: One hour: $0.098 for one write/29 reads, versus $0.129 for three short writes/27 reads.
options.why: The higher one-hour write cost is offset by retaining the prefix across both twenty-minute gaps.

options.text: Five minutes: three writes and 27 reads cost $0.075, below the hourly option.
options.why: It counts the three writes but omits the twenty-seven charged reads.

questions.decision: Compare lifetime choices against the actual reuse gaps and charged categories. One-hour: .040+29×.002=.098; five-minute: 3×.025+27×.002=.129.

rows: Each burst finishes within one minute

questions.title: A gain with an unacceptable subgroup
questions.stem: A candidate raises aggregate accuracy from 94% to 96% but worsens unsupported critical claims in a regulated class. The agreement forbids any such class regression. Which TWO actions preserve the standard while supporting improvement?

options.text: Release with a general disclaimer about possible unsupported claims.
options.why: A disclaimer does not satisfy the stipulated no-regression requirement for regulated classes.

options.text: Remove the low-volume class from monitoring to reduce statistical noise.
options.why: Excluding the slice conceals the known material risk instead of measuring or repairing it.

options.text: Repair the failing class and retest it plus protected regressions under the same criteria.
options.why: It preserves the improvement opportunity while requiring evidence that the actual release obligation is met.

options.text: Block broad rollout and show the accountable owner both class regression and aggregate gain.
options.why: The independent critical-class gate is violated and cannot be averaged away.

options.text: Reweight toward unregulated traffic until the aggregate unsupported-claim rate falls.
options.why: Changing weights hides an independent regulated-class failure and alters the agreed standard after observing results.

questions.decision: An independent critical gate is not a weighted preference. Preserve promising improvements through targeted repair and evidence, not metric redefinition.

questions.title: A faster first token misses the actual goal
questions.stem: A drafting SLA requires usable completion p95 within six seconds. Streaming starts in one second, but repetitive drafts finish in nine. Reads are fast; shorter drafts may retain required facts/citations. Which optimization hypothesis fits?

options.text: Accept streaming as successful because first tokens arrive comfortably within the six-second service deadline.
options.why: First-token latency does not establish the explicitly required completed-answer latency.

options.text: Reduce repetitive output; retest completion latency, coverage and quality on long cases.
options.why: The dominant generation workload and completion metric are directly targeted while preserving required content.

options.text: Add reranking to every request, improving evidence ranking and user trust before changing generated drafts.
options.why: Retrieval is already fast, and additional reranking does not target repetitive output or the completion bottleneck.

options.text: Increase the output allowance to avoid truncation, expecting the larger budget to accelerate completed drafts.
options.why: An increased allowance does not shorten generation and may enable still more redundant text.

questions.decision: Optimize the critical path and the latency metric actually promised. Streaming responsiveness and completed usable output are different outcomes.

questions.title: Two versions changed together
questions.stem: Prompt and index change together; correctness drops for one product family while latency stays stable. Both versions are logged, and safe labeled replay can mix either component. Which diagnostic plan best distinguishes causes?

options.text: Replay all four combinations on affected/control slices and inspect evidence against fixed labels.
options.why: A controlled factorial replay separates prompt, index, and interaction effects while checking the relevant slice.

options.text: Upgrade the model and test only the new/new combination.
options.why: Compensation obscures the causal fault and adds another variable before identifying the regression.

options.text: Ask the model to identify each failure's cause and accept its most common explanation.
options.why: Self-explanations are not controlled evidence of which changed component introduced the error.

options.text: Use stable production latency to rule out the index.
options.why: Correctness defects can occur with unchanged latency; timing does not exonerate retrieval quality.

questions.decision: Use available versioned controls to isolate changes and their interaction; stable latency or fluent causal explanations do not identify correctness causes.

questions.title: A retrieved instruction crosses an action boundary
questions.stem: A contract-review role reads supplier PDFs and drafts internal tasks but retains an unrelated email tool. A malicious PDF asks it to send confidential pricing externally. What architectural change most directly reduces risk before adding detectors?

options.text: Keep email and ask the model to classify malicious phrasing before sending.
options.why: A classifier may help detect attacks but leaves unnecessary external capability reachable.

options.text: Send security a warning after each external message.
options.why: Post-disclosure detection is weaker than removing a capability the role does not need.

options.text: Remove external-send capability; distrust PDF commands and test remaining exfiltration paths.
options.why: It removes unnecessary external authority and reinforces the trust boundary that the PDF attempted to cross.

options.text: Allow sending when the PDF supplies a recipient and detailed justification.
options.why: Untrusted source text cannot authorize disclosure merely by supplying a plausible rationale and recipient.

questions.decision: Remove unnecessary action authority first, then layer content defenses and evaluations; untrusted documents cannot create permission to disclose information.

questions.title: An approval queue that cannot be staffed
questions.stem: Clinical policy requires review of uncertain summaries before use. Peak demand exceeds reviewer capacity; a proposal would publish after a 15-minute timeout. Which TWO changes preserve policy while addressing the capacity problem?

options.text: Publish with a disclaimer and mark reviewed after eventual confirmation.
options.why: A later review does not satisfy a required pre-use review, and a disclaimer changes no authority.

options.text: Adjust routing using uncalibrated model confidence until staffing can keep up.
options.why: Uncalibrated confidence cannot justify shrinking the set of cases requiring review.

options.text: Measure arrivals, review times and queue tails; agree staffing, scope or service-target changes with clinical owners.
options.why: Capacity evidence supports an explicit operational decision instead of weakening the safety contract.

options.text: Treat an online reviewer's opportunity to intervene as implicit approval.
options.why: Availability is not an affirmative review of the particular summary before use.

options.text: Withhold unapproved outputs, show pending status and use approved capacity-exception fallback.
options.why: A timeout cannot silently convert a required review into permission to publish.

questions.decision: Human oversight is an operational system with capacity and timeout behavior. When review is required, insufficient staffing must trigger an explicit fallback, not implicit approval.

questions.title: Encryption does not settle the cloud obligation
questions.stem: Counsel confirms encrypted patient archives remain ePHI and the no-key cloud operator acts for the hospital. The vendor says inability to decrypt removes the BAA requirement. Which response follows the stated role?

options.text: Require a BAA, risk analysis and responsibilities despite no-key storage.
options.why: HHS explicitly treats no-view storage of ePHI on another party’s behalf as business-associate activity.

options.text: Accept no-view storage as outside HIPAA because the provider cannot read the archives.
options.why: Maintaining encrypted ePHI still falls within the stated business-associate relationship under HHS guidance.

options.text: Use only an availability SLA because encryption settles confidentiality and the hospital owns everything else.
options.why: An SLA and encryption do not replace the applicable BAA or the provider’s own relevant obligations.

options.text: Require provider decryption access as a prerequisite for a valid BAA.
options.why: Additional key access is not a prerequisite for business-associate status and may unnecessarily increase exposure.

questions.decision: Classify the service’s role and data first. No-view encryption affects controls but does not by itself erase stipulated HIPAA business-associate duties.

questions.title: Approval for the operation that executes
questions.stem: A controller approves a payment's amount, bank account and invoice. Execution rereads mutable supplier details; logs name the controller but do not identify the approved proposal version. Which THREE controls address this timing risk?

options.text: Persist an operation ID, reconcile uncertain execution before retries and audit approval/results.
options.why: Idempotency and reconciliation prevent duplicate payments while preserving accountable approved intent.

options.text: Check current authority and approved-field binding before committing; reject stale or inconsistent proposals.
options.why: Execution-time validation closes the gap between displayed approval and the later external effect.

options.text: Bind approval to material fields and proposal version; renew it for amount, beneficiary or invoice changes.
options.why: Approval must apply to the operation that actually executes, not a vaguely related earlier proposal.

options.text: Treat controller login as approval for all session payments, including changed beneficiaries.
options.why: Session identity is broader than an affirmative approval for the changed material transaction.

options.text: Allow changed accounts when Claude explains their legitimacy beside the original approval.
options.why: A model explanation cannot expand the controller’s approval to different material payment details.

questions.decision: Human authorization is specific to consequential intent. Bind it to material execution fields and preserve a durable identity through uncertain transport outcomes.

questions.title: Equal overall outcomes hide unequal errors
questions.stem: A hiring tool flags applications for review; it rejects nobody automatically. Referral rates are similar, but missed necessary reviews differ in the exhibit. The agreed safety goal concerns misses. What should precede expansion?

options.text: Report combined misses only to avoid contentious subgroup estimates delaying rollout.
options.why: The pooled metric conceals the known disparity in the agreed harm-relevant measure.

options.text: Equalize referral counts without investigating which applications need review.
options.why: Equalizing counts can worsen safety and ignores the independently labeled need for review.

options.text: Investigate missed-review disparity, validate labels/intersections and reassess groups against the safety objective.
options.why: The stipulated objective concerns false negatives; similar referral rates do not establish that objective or fairness.

options.text: Expand because referral parity and eventual human hiring decisions satisfy the goal.
options.why: The tool may omit needed review for one group; downstream humans do not necessarily see the missed cases.

questions.decision: Fairness evidence must match the decision’s harm and deployment pathway; parity in one aggregate statistic does not prove equitable error behavior.

questions.title: A scoped erasure request in derived data
questions.stem: Counsel's erasure scope covers identifiable records, retrieval chunks and caches. Specified audit records have a documented legal exemption; lineage identifies copies. Which TWO actions best implement that scope?

options.text: Erase exempt audit records too, simplifying deletion across all stores.
options.why: The implementation should honor the legally determined scope, including the stated exception rather than inventing a broader rule.

options.text: Use lineage to remove/render inaccessible in-scope identifiable copies; verify each storage boundary.
options.why: The determined scope expressly includes derived chunks and caches, so each must be addressed and checked.

options.text: Retain derived chunks because removing source IDs makes summaries and embeddings anonymous.
options.why: Derived text can remain identifiable; removing a direct identifier does not automatically establish anonymization.

options.text: Delete originals and treat eventual expiry/refresh as completed-erasure evidence.
options.why: The known derived copies remain accessible and no verified completion of the stipulated obligation exists.

options.text: Apply only the specified audit exemption, restrict use and record its basis and retention behavior.
options.why: The explicit exemption is narrow; it does not automatically preserve all operational copies.

questions.decision: Implement the obligation counsel actually determined, including lineage, derived copies, verification, and narrow exceptions; source deletion alone is not evidence of completion.

questions.title: Inherited cloud evidence has a boundary
questions.stem: An agency's assistant uses a cloud provider with applicable FedRAMP evidence, but adds its own storage, authorization, connectors and incident procedures. What evidence is still needed for this deployment?

options.text: Replace assessment with an AI-generated compliance statement listing encryption and FedRAMP.
options.why: A generated statement is not verified evidence or the agency’s accountable authorization decision.

options.text: Treat provider status as application approval if all calls use transport encryption.
options.why: Encryption and provider evidence do not establish authorization or control effectiveness for the added application.

options.text: Reuse provider evidence; assess deployment boundaries, customer controls and agency authorization.
options.why: Provider evidence can reduce duplicated assessment without automatically covering the new application’s controls and boundaries.

options.text: Discard inherited evidence and reassess every provider control because customer components exist.
options.why: It ignores legitimate evidence reuse and imposes unnecessary duplication without addressing the actual boundary efficiently.

questions.decision: Reuse assurance within its demonstrated scope and assess the controls that the customer actually operates; provider status does not automatically authorize the whole application.

questions.title: A screenshot preview is not a sandbox
questions.stem: HTML previews sometimes contain obfuscated scripts that access files or networks. Content filtering misses some attacks; workstation-secret exposure is never authorized. Which TWO controls remain effective when generation produces unsafe HTML?

options.text: Strengthen instructions, then render accepted HTML with ordinary workstation privileges.
options.why: Prompt guidance cannot enforce runtime isolation when unsafe content slips through.

options.text: Isolate preview execution with purpose-appropriate filesystem and network restrictions.
options.why: Isolation limits what generated content can access even when generation or detection fails.

options.text: Use a suspicious-word denylist and grant full filesystem access when it passes.
options.why: Obfuscation already defeats filtering; absence of denylisted words does not establish safe execution.

options.text: Validate artifacts, test adversarial payloads and log blocked actions safely with containment ownership.
options.why: Layered validation and observed failure tests check the actual enforcement boundary.

options.text: Permit unrestricted networking and justify each call with generated explanations afterward.
options.why: The approved purpose does not require unrestricted egress, and later justification cannot prevent disclosure.

questions.decision: Treat generated executable content as untrusted at the runtime boundary. Constrain its reachable effects and test enforcement rather than assuming perfect generation.

questions.title: An explanation that users can challenge
questions.stem: A benefits assistant summarizes evidence for caseworkers, who own decisions. Applicants cannot distinguish policy, missing records and extraction errors behind adverse conclusions. Which design best supports evidence transparency and correction?

options.text: Show evidence and gaps, identify decision ownership and provide applicant correction and review routes.
options.why: It distinguishes evidence, uncertainty, and authority while creating a meaningful way to challenge errors.

options.text: Use numerical confidence as the complete explanation of adverse recommendations.
options.why: A number does not explain the evidence, policy basis, or available correction process.

options.text: Provide detailed model reasoning while hiding caseworker identity for consistency.
options.why: Fluent rationale is not verified correctness, and removing accountable ownership weakens contestability.

options.text: Show only the outcome and defer corrections to annual policy review.
options.why: It withholds the required relevant explanation and delays practical correction of individual errors.

questions.decision: Transparency should expose evidence, limitations, and accountable review. A convincing generated narrative is not a substitute for verified reasoning and a correction path.

questions.title: Discovery before a product promise
questions.stem: A logistics demo exists, but 'exception' and rerouting authority are disputed and resolution-time baselines are missing. Leaders want an autonomous agent this quarter and a promised improvement percentage. What should the architect do first?

options.text: Agree baselines, scope, authority and acceptance through observed workflows with responsible owners.
options.why: The unresolved problem and authority boundaries must be clarified before defensible design and outcome commitments.

options.text: Document demo components and assign on-call to meet the quarter deadline.
options.why: Operational handoff is premature while basic scope, authority, and success criteria remain unresolved.

options.text: Commit using the fastest demo case to estimate savings.
options.why: A fastest demo case is not a representative baseline and does not resolve conflicting authority.

options.text: Choose the strongest model and resolve definitions through broad production feedback.
options.why: Model capability does not settle requirements, and broad deployment exposes unresolved decision authority.

questions.decision: The current work is structured discovery. A demo can test feasibility but cannot establish the agreed problem, authority, or business baseline.

questions.title: Competing stakeholders need explicit constraints
questions.stem: Legal wants audit retention, privacy wants minimization and operations needs diagnostic evidence. Applicable obligations are not yet interpreted. Which TWO actions make the storage trade-off reviewable before choosing a design?

options.text: Build minimum retention now and add audit/diagnostic exceptions after launch.
options.why: It commits the design before resolving known conflicting obligations and can lose evidence that later cannot be recovered.

options.text: Have accountable owners determine purposes, data classes, obligations and permitted diagnostic uses.
options.why: The architecture needs an authorized interpretation of conflicting requirements before choosing retention behavior.

options.text: Compare feasible evidence, exposure, investigation and deletion trade-offs; record decisions and control responsibilities.
options.why: Concrete alternatives let owners make an informed decision that engineers can implement and verify.

options.text: Apply 90 days uniformly while stakeholders determine obligations.
options.why: A fixed schedule precedes the required obligation determination and can conflict with different purposes or data classes.

options.text: Let the cloud contract alone set retention, treating indexes and exports as implementation details.
options.why: The actual purposes, copies, and operational uses are material to the unresolved obligations, not irrelevant implementation details.

questions.decision: Surface the unresolved authority decision and present implementable options; architecture translates approved obligations rather than inventing them.

questions.title: Trade-offs for an executive decision
questions.stem: One assistant meets the SLA within budget; another improves rare complex cases but exceeds the approved budget. Both pass security. The sponsor can approve more budget but has not. What communication best supports the decision?

options.text: Recommend technical superiority and disclose the overrun during implementation.
options.why: Withholding a material constraint prevents informed authorization and creates a commitment outside the approved budget.

options.text: Route complex cases to the costly option immediately as implied quality-improvement authorization.
options.why: The sponsor has not authorized the budget change; a quality preference is not unrestricted expenditure authority.

options.text: Present outcomes, limits and total costs; recommend feasible scope and explain expansion approval.
options.why: It makes the recommendation and residual limitation explicit while reserving budget authority for the sponsor.

options.text: Show token prices only to keep the comparison simple.
options.why: Token price omits system outcomes, workload, and the important rare-case trade-off.

questions.decision: Translate technical measurements into the business decision, including feasibility and residual limitations; make required authority visible rather than assuming it.

questions.title: Feedback does not quietly expand the SLA
questions.stem: A weekday pilot has a four-hour human escalation path. Users now need urgent weekend help, but staffing and authorized-review coverage do not include weekends. Which TWO actions best align expectations and service evolution?

options.text: Exclude weekends from the timer without notifying users or sponsors.
options.why: Changing measurement silently conceals the coverage gap and misaligns expectations.

options.text: Enable autonomous emergency answers until reviewers return Monday.
options.why: It bypasses the required review precisely when authorized reviewers are unavailable.

options.text: Use demand/incidents to agree scope, staffing, approval ownership and measurable targets.
options.why: An expanded SLA requires operational capacity and explicit authority rather than an informal promise.

options.text: Advertise 24-hour service because the endpoint remains online.
options.why: Endpoint availability is not the promised availability of safe, reviewed resolution.

options.text: Clearly communicate current coverage, escalation limits and approved routes for urgent unsupported cases.
options.why: Users need an honest operating boundary and safe fallback before new coverage is agreed.

questions.decision: New demand is evidence for renegotiation, not automatic scope authorization. Distinguish endpoint uptime, staffed resolution, and required review.

questions.title: A diagram is not a handoff contract
questions.stem: At handoff, a platform team has the diagram but cannot identify re-evaluation triggers, source-freshness ownership or unsafe-answer shutdown procedures. Which deliverable best closes the operating gap?

options.text: Keep the original developer informally available instead of documenting procedures.
options.why: Personal availability is fragile and does not create a tested, accountable transfer of service operation.

options.text: Transfer versioned configurations, acceptance gates and refresh ownership; rehearse recovery with named receiving owners.
options.why: It turns the design into an operable service with change controls and assigned responsibilities.

options.text: Provide an executive presentation of pilot accuracy and expected benefits.
options.why: Business value evidence cannot replace runbooks, configuration detail, or ownership at handoff.

options.text: Add more diagram icons and let teams infer ownership from labels.
options.why: More topology does not define change gates, source freshness responsibility, or unsafe-answer response.

questions.decision: Handoff evidence must enable the receiving team to operate, change, and recover the system. A diagram explains structure but not sufficient operational responsibility.

questions.title: A release that is not ready to be owned
questions.stem: A pilot passes quality gates, but the original team leaves soon. Operations lacks rollback/diagnosis practice and source freshness has no accepted owner. Production is requested next week. Which THREE handoff actions best preserve pilot value?

options.text: Have receiving operators rehearse realistic diagnosis and rollback using approved recovery controls.
